Yes, there are.

However the majority of philosophical questions you hear discussed are not really difficult ones, just ones where people are misunderstanding language.

For example: is there free will? This is an invalid question as free will is never defined.

Why are we here? This one confuses the different definitions of "why" (how did it come to be vs for what purpose).

Once you actually define your terms, most philosophical questions are easy to answer very definitively.

If there is, I've never encountered one.

I suppose philosophy is like art. Neither will ever lead you to a solid conclusion, but they can be rewarding nonetheless. They can also get pretty tiring, too, depending on your outlook.

There are some things that were originally philosophical questions that crossed into more rigorous fields, such as information theory. I have only the most passing familiarity with this stuff but I recall that there is a mathematical proof for what is essentially the assertion that it is impossible to communicate precisely with another human being. There is no way to use words that have rock-solid meanings, and no way to fix that problem either. It has to do with set completeness or some such.

I guess its kind of like that joke about alternative medicine - once you can pin it down and prove it, it's not alternative any more, it's just medicine. Once you can bring a mathematical proof to bear on a philosophical assertion, then it's not philosophy any more.

Philosophy is like Lego, each block is a sound argument, as you study philosophy and learn these pieces of logic or think through arguments you gain more and more blocks.

You can use these Lego blocks to argue for things that are metaphysical or are false (a thought experiment) like asking "can I survive the death of my body" (nothing logically wrong with this question as it separates I from the body implying a soul or something similar), as opposed to asking "can I survive death" (death implies no survival) so to argue for things that science cannot observe (currently) we can use those Lego blocks to build a case in a logical manner or at least ask the right question and it is in these areas where the answers are hard.

There are also many thought traps aka fallacies that are superficially sound but deeply incorrect and often the victim of those traps can be unaware of their wrongness and their truth is, in reality, 2=2=4 this is called A non sequitur. Reference YouTube commenters for further reading regarding fallacies.
